blocks.text: Esther 10 contains 3 verses. It opens with: And the king Ahasuerus laid a tribute upon the land, and upon the isles of the sea. It concludes with: For Mordecai the Jew was next unto king Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews, and accepted of the multitude of his brethren, seeking the good of his people, and speaking peace to all his seed. Supplied contextual evidence for this passage adds: Esther displays informed Persian color alongside stylization, satire, repeated improbability, exact symmetry, and dramatic reversal. Labels such as history, historical novella, comedy, court tale, and festival etiology describe different features; none should be treated as a neutral conclusion that resolves all historical questions. Greek Esther is not merely the Hebrew story with isolated devotional glosses: its forms expand, relocate, and interpret the narrative through dreams, prayers, divine naming, and fuller documents. Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and Jewish readers therefore encounter materially different canonical forms.
